message: It won't really work for medium to big sizes organisations, spinning up an internal team to manage/oversee the requirements, implementation, UX and cutover. Plus ongoing maintenance. Plus years of edge cases that the existing software has built up. Change management. Plus the risk adverse nature in most organisations across every aspect. For smaller organisations though, it can work.

author: gk0563
message: OMG, <@272654283919458306> — I'm so stoked you're doing this!  I made a 7m video for you, and open letter to you and the people jamming on this!  First off, Swyx, congrats on all your fantastic achievements — World Fair was amazing!!!  Last week, I was so excited to see this contest. I remember poking around last week on Twitter trying to figure out which tool you wanted to replace — and I was delighted to learn this morning that it's Sessionboard, a CFP management tool, which is a category of tools I've loved to hate for almost fifteen years.  Over that time, we've used five of the worst tools on the planet to run our conferences, and we were held hostage to every one of them. This is something I have a tremendous amount of passion for.   I've literally written workarounds for this terrible category of tools since 2014 -- Trello, Zapier, Google Sheets, and an entire app to rewrite the submission review process.  On Saturday, after I read your "Kill My SaaS" posts, I did some digging.  I used Claude Code with Fable to go through more than 20,000 Slack messages from the past 12–13 years of running Enterprise AI Summit (and its predecessors: DevOps Enterprise Summit, Enterprise Technology Leadership Summit).  I wanted to put this together for you to:  - show you how important this is to me — it's literally a problem I've been struggling with for 12 years - my goal is to get a mini-CFP launched today for the Enterprise AI Summit in Charlotte, NC (Oct 7-8) -- our existing process and tools were just heavy enough of a lift to make me, until yesterday, say "screw it, let's just use Basecamp" (hahaha!) - Swyx, I have some questions for you and your team — maybe this is a tool that you'll want to use.  If it differs sufficiently from my process, maybe it won't - if your CFP session closely matches mine, I'm all in on this competition — even though I'm starting one day late — and if I win (hey, can always dream!), I'll donate the $10K prize to STEM charity - and I wanted to share the 12+ year history of the tools (almost all terrible, one was amazing but went out of business, and one is tolerable, but I ended up writing a whole new front-end by scraping its contents) — and I wanted to share some of the interesting economics of this software category

author: gk0563
message: Question to you and the team:  On scale of 1-10, which ethos mostly matches your CFP reviewer process:  1=NeurIPS (blind: no one sees anything except their queue) , 10=committee of friends (everyone seems everything)  1. Academic tier — HotCRP / EasyChair / OpenReview (the far pole)  ```    paper ──▶ bidding ──▶ assignment (3 reviewers/paper, conflicts checked)           ──▶ independent double-blind reviews (structured scores + text)           ──▶ author rebuttal ──▶ reviewer discussion (per-paper, gated)           ──▶ PC meeting / meta-review ──▶ decision ``` - Shape: due process.** Justified when reviewers number in the hundreds and fairness-at-scale is the product. This is the tradition Sessionize/Sessionboard unconsciously imitate — for committees of nine who all read everything anyway.  10. Everyone sees everything  ``` SPEAKER                    THE SYSTEM                       COMMITTEE (all 9, no assignments) ───────                    ──────────                       ───────────────────────────────── one-page /proposals/new    New Proposal email ──────────▶   FULL proposal lands in inbox: no account required   ──▶  (everything inline)              title, abstract, every custom markdown abstract                                           field, speaker bio + headshot, + "Notes to the Planning                                    prior-talk video link, comments   Committee" (private) ──▶ one orange button:               so far. Read it over coffee. + co-speakers (repeatable  [View, Comment, and Rate »]           │   block, avatar upload)                                          ▼                            comment ⇄ email loop:            rate privately (per-organizer), speaker can comment   ◀──▶ every comment re-emails all;     comment publicly-to-committee on own proposal            reply-by-email works;            ("[pc]" convention for                            "Click here to reply"            committee-only remarks)                                  │                                  ▼                            accepted → activity → drag-n-drop onto proportional                            schedule grid (pixels_per_minute) → published at                            <event>.busyconf.com/schedule + /mobile (offline-capable                            HTML5) + embed — "hosted forever" ```

author: fabianhertwig
message: my agent would have some questions for your agent who's digging through slack and mail :D. Would you be willing to share more insights?  > Your four posts map five territories in depth — review, scheduling, data longevity, the chase, employer approval. So no follow-ups there. Five questions about what the posts do not touch: > The decision itself. When the committee finally picks, what actually decides — average score, one champion arguing, topic balance ("we need one Kubernetes talk"), speaker diversity, sponsor pressure? And what would a tool have to put on the screen in that meeting to be used live, instead of everyone looking at a spreadsheet? > The rejected majority. For every acceptance there are several rejections. What does the archive show happening after the rejection letters go out — replies, requests for feedback, anger, people resubmitting the next year? Is there anything a tool could do for that group that would actually matter? > Sponsors and the program. Sponsored talks, "the gold sponsor gets a keynote slot," vendor pitches in the CFP pile — how did that collide with the committee's process, and did any tool ever model it, or was it all handled in side conversations? > The final 72 hours. What breaks in the last three days before doors open — no-shows, room swaps, AV surprises, schedule reprints — and who fixes it with what? Is there a moment where the CFP tool is abandoned entirely and everything moves to phones? > The one you stopped noticing. For your agent, verbatim: across the entire archive, what is the most frequently recurring problem or time-sink that none of the four posts mentioned? We read them carefully — we want the pain that has become invisible to you.
